claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy has a homogeneous distribution of alloying elements, including passivating species.
The initial high-entropy alloy has a coarse-grained microstructure.
Mechanical wear promotes refinement of the alloy's surface microstructure.
Wear-induced grain refinement produces localized surface enrichment of passivating elements.
Surface refinement exposes regions enriched in passivating elements.
Passivating-element enrichment accelerates protective oxide-film formation.
Passivating-element enrichment sustains dynamic regeneration of a self-healing passive film during wear.
Dynamic passive-film regeneration reduces further simultaneous mechanical and chemical degradation.
Combined wear and corrosion will produce a lower total degradation rate than the sum of degradation measured under isolated wear and isolated corrosion.
Isolated wear or isolated corrosion will not exhibit the proposed synergistic mitigation.
The proposed effect requires an alloy containing sufficient passivating elements.
Moderate wear can induce beneficial grain refinement without gross material failure.
The proposed effect may fail in alloys lacking significant passivating species.
Extreme wear may cause catastrophic damage rather than beneficial microstructural adaptation.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes surface refinement to mechanical wear itself, whereas the baseline describes isolated-wear tests as lacking the beneficial surface modifications associated with simultaneous loading. Because isolated wear still applies mechanical wear, the asserted absence of those modifications is in tension with the proposed causal trigger.
